title: What actually fixed "the AI forgot my story": we stopped storing history as text
author: No-Pollution7797
selftext:
I've been building an AI text-adventure platform for about a year, and the single problem that ate the most engineering time was the one every player complains about: the model forgets. I want to write up what didn't work, because I think the failure mode is more interesting than the fix.

**What didn't work: summarising harder.**
The obvious move is to compress the transcript as it grows. We did this, tuned it repeatedly, and players still reported drift. The reason is that summarisation is lossy in exactly the wrong direction — it preserves plot and discards specifics. "You travelled to the capital and met the merchant" survives; "you gave her your mother's ring" does not. But the ring is the thing the player cared about. We were systematically deleting the emotionally load-bearing details and keeping the scaffolding.

**What didn't work: bigger context.**
Longer windows delayed the problem by hours and made every turn slower and more expensive. It also made a second failure worse — with 40k tokens of history in the prompt, the model started referencing *irrelevant* old events, which reads as a different kind of broken.

**What worked: stop storing history as text at all.**
Now an action produces a structured outcome, and that outcome is written into world state — relationships, faction standing, entity facts, events attached to specific places and people. Retrieval then assembles a prompt from what's relevant to your current location, who's present, and recent history, rather than from a rolling transcript.

Concretely, that means the ring is a fact attached to a character, not a sentence competing for context. Twenty sessions later the NPC can raise it, because retrieving it costs a lookup rather than a slot in a window.

Things that surprised me along the way:

- **Consequences you didn't notice are the valuable ones.** With a manual lorebook/world-info approach, only facts the player thought to write down persist. State-based capture keeps things the player improvised and forgot — which is what makes callbacks feel uncanny rather than mechanical.
- **The world needs to move when nobody is watching.** We run simulation ticks that advance factions and conflicts between sessions. This did more for "the world feels alive" than any prompt engineering.
- **Ripple effects need hard caps.** Letting consequences propagate freely through the entity graph was great for two hops and incoherent by four. We bounded traversal depth. Emergence is good; unbounded emergence is noise.
- **The tone of the narrator matters less than whether it remembers.** We spent a lot on prose quality early. Retention moved on continuity, not style.

Happy to go deeper on any part — the retrieval assembly and the tick pipeline are the parts I'd most like to compare notes on with people solving this differently.

(Disclosure: this is my product. Mods, flaired as Commercial Self Promotion per rule 4. Not linking it in the body — it's in my profile if anyone wants it.)

comments.author: witmann_pl
comments.body: So much text and you failed to explain what you actually do to store that data.

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
We didn't store memories as text 
— we stored them as text, formatted differently.  No paragraphs of markdown, just blocks of 30-50 words in a machine legible file format.
